title: Glossary
line: Essential investing terms, each mapped to the TEI curriculum.

items.def: Something that has economic value and can provide future benefits.
items.why: Investors allocate capital between different assets based on expected return and risk.
items.example: Shares, bonds, property, businesses, and cash are all examples of assets.

items.def: The process of committing capital with the expectation of receiving future benefits.
items.why: Investment is ownership. Understanding this distinguishes investing from trading or speculating.
items.example: Buying a share means owning part of a business, not simply holding a number that moves up and down.

items.def: Buying an asset primarily because you expect someone else will pay more later.
items.why: Investment asks whether a business will create value. Speculation asks only whether the price will rise. Recognising which one you are doing protects against costly mistakes.

items.def: The possibility that an outcome differs from expectations.
items.why: Risk is not simply volatility. Real risk includes permanent capital loss, poor decisions, and overpaying.

items.def: The gain or loss generated from an investment.
items.example: Sources of return include price appreciation, dividends, and interest.

items.def: Generating returns on previous returns.
items.why: Small improvements become significant over long periods, because each period's gains build on top of the last.
items.example: Capital, return, and time combine multiplicatively: the same rate of return sustained over a longer time horizon produces disproportionately larger results.

items.def: The total income generated from selling products or services.
items.example: A company selling one million products at £10 each generates £10 million in revenue.

items.def: Revenue minus the direct costs of producing goods or services.
items.why: Shows the economics of the product.
items.example: Revenue minus cost of goods sold.

items.def: Gross profit expressed as a percentage of revenue.
items.why: Higher margins often indicate stronger economics.
items.example: Gross profit divided by revenue.

items.def: Profit generated from normal business operations.
items.example: Gross profit minus operating expenses.

items.def: The final profit after all expenses, taxes, and costs.
Movement of money into and out of a business.
items.why: Profits do not always equal cash generation.

items.def: Cash remaining after operating expenses and required investment.
items.why: Businesses are ultimately valued by their ability to generate cash.
items.example: Operating cash flow minus capital expenditure.

items.def: A statement showing that a company's assets equal its liabilities plus shareholders' equity.
The total value assigned to a company by the stock market.
items.example: A £20 share price multiplied by one billion shares outstanding gives a £20 billion market cap.

items.def: A measure of company value that includes debt.
items.why: Provides a fuller picture than market cap alone.
items.example: Market cap plus debt minus cash.

items.def: A valuation ratio comparing share price to earnings.
items.example: A £100 share price against £5 earnings per share gives a P/E of 20.

items.def: Profit allocated to each company share.
items.example: Net income divided by shares outstanding.

items.def: A valuation measure comparing company value to revenue.
items.why: Useful for valuing companies with low or negative profits.

items.def: A valuation method estimating the present value of future cash flows.
items.why: Future money is worth less than money today.

items.def: The estimated true economic value of a business.
items.why: Price and value can differ.

items.def: How a company creates, delivers, and captures value.
items.example: Who pays, why do they pay, and how does the company make money.

items.def: A factor allowing a company to outperform its competitors.
items.example: Brand, network effects, cost advantage, and switching costs are common sources.

items.def: A durable competitive advantage that protects a company's profits.
items.why: A moat protects long-term profits from competition. The term was popularised by Warren Buffett.
items.example: Coca-Cola's brand and Visa's payment network are commonly cited examples.

items.def: The ability to increase prices without losing customers.
items.why: A strong indicator of business quality.

items.def: A product that becomes more valuable as more users join it.
items.example: Payment networks and marketplaces are common examples.

items.def: The difficulty customers face when changing providers.
items.example: Software systems and banking relationships are common sources of switching costs.

items.def: Spreading investments across different assets.
items.why: Reduces unnecessary risk.

items.def: How capital is divided between different asset classes.
items.example: Equities, bonds, cash, and property are the main asset classes capital is divided between.

items.def: The percentage of a portfolio invested in one asset.
items.why: Controls risk.

items.def: Holding fewer investments with larger allocations to each.
items.why: Concentration increases exposure to an investor's highest-conviction ideas, but it also increases company-specific risk.

items.def: Adjusting a portfolio back toward its intended allocations.
A prolonged period of rising asset prices.
A prolonged period of declining asset prices.
The repeated pattern markets move through over time.
items.example: Expansion, optimism, excess, decline, and recovery.

items.def: The degree to which prices move.
items.why: Volatility is not automatically risk.

items.def: How easily an asset can be bought or sold.
A measure of how efficiently a company turns invested capital into profits.
items.why: High ROIC businesses often have strong competitive advantages, efficient operations, and better capital allocation.
items.example: Operating profit after tax divided by invested capital.

items.def: A measure of how effectively a company generates profit from shareholders' equity.
items.why: Useful for comparing businesses, but a high ROE caused by excessive debt can be misleading.
items.example: Net income divided by shareholders' equity.

items.def: A measure of how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate profit.
items.example: Net income divided by total assets.

items.def: How management decides where to deploy company resources.
items.why: A great business with poor capital allocation can destroy value.
items.example: Reinvestment, acquisitions, debt reduction, dividends, and share buybacks.

items.def: The impact of fixed costs on profitability.
items.why: When revenue grows, companies with high operating leverage can see profits increase rapidly. The opposite happens when revenue declines.

items.def: Using debt to increase potential returns.
items.why: Financial leverage can amplify growth, but it can equally amplify losses.

items.def: A measure comparing company debt to shareholder equity.
items.why: Shows a company's reliance on borrowed capital.

items.def: Measures a company's ability to pay its interest costs.
items.why: Higher ratios generally indicate stronger debt capacity.
items.example: Operating profit divided by interest expense.

items.def: The total potential market opportunity for a product or service.
items.why: A large TAM can create opportunity, but large markets do not guarantee successful companies.

items.def: The portion of the total addressable market a company can realistically target.
The percentage of an industry controlled by a company.
items.why: Increasing market share can indicate competitive strength.

items.def: The profitability of one unit of business activity.
items.why: The key question is whether growth creates value or whether it creates losses.
items.example: One customer, one subscription, or one product sale.

items.def: The cost of acquiring a new customer.
items.example: Sales and marketing costs divided by new customers.

items.def: The estimated value of a customer relationship over time.
items.why: A healthy business usually has a lifetime value greater than its acquisition cost.

items.def: The percentage of customers who leave over time.
items.why: Low churn often indicates customer satisfaction, product strength, and switching costs.

items.def: Revenue expected to repeat consistently.
items.why: Creates predictability.
items.example: Subscriptions, memberships, and contracts.

items.def: A meeting where management discusses financial results with analysts and investors.
items.why: Useful for analysing management communication, strategy, and risks.

items.def: Management's forecast for future performance.
items.why: Guidance is information, not certainty.

items.def: The percentage of company shares owned by executives, founders, or directors.
items.why: Can indicate alignment between management and shareholders.

items.def: Shares available for public trading.
items.why: Lower float can increase price volatility.

items.def: A reduction in existing shareholders' ownership percentage.
items.example: Issuing new shares, stock-based compensation, and fundraising are common causes.

items.def: A company purchasing its own shares.
items.why: Buybacks reduce share count and increase the ownership percentage of remaining shareholders, but they destroy value if the shares bought back are overpriced.

items.def: Payments made by companies to shareholders.
items.why: Represents one method of returning capital to shareholders.

items.def: Annual dividend expressed as a percentage of share price.
items.example: Dividend divided by share price.

items.def: The decline in purchasing power caused by rising prices.
items.example: Affects interest rates, valuations, and consumer behaviour.

items.def: The cost of borrowing money.
items.example: Influences company valuations, consumer spending, and asset prices.

items.def: Actions taken by central banks to influence money supply and interest rates.
items.example: Interest rate changes and asset purchases are common tools.

items.def: Government decisions involving spending and taxation.
The total value of goods and services produced by an economy.
A significant decline in economic activity.
items.why: Different businesses respond differently during recessions.

items.def: The percentage of people actively seeking work who are unemployed.
Investing in businesses believed to be trading below their intrinsic value.
items.example: Associated with investors such as Benjamin Graham and Warren Buffett.

items.def: Investing in companies expected to grow earnings significantly.
items.why: Growth must justify the valuation paid for it.

items.def: Investing in businesses with strong economics, durable advantages, and high returns on capital.
Investing based on trends in price or earnings strength.
Investing in a broad market index rather than selecting individual companies.
items.why: Offers low cost and diversification.

items.def: Return above a benchmark after adjusting for risk.
A measure of an asset's sensitivity to market movements.
items.why: Higher beta does not automatically mean higher risk.

items.def: A measure of return relative to volatility.
items.example: Return minus the risk-free rate, divided by volatility.

items.def: A strategy that profits when an asset price falls.
items.why: Potential losses can be unlimited.

items.def: A demand for additional capital when leveraged positions fall in value.
items.why: Leverage can force decisions at the worst possible time.

items.def: Financial contracts giving the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an asset at a set price.
Long-term options contracts, usually lasting more than one year.
items.why: Allows leveraged exposure but introduces additional risks.

items.def: Financial instruments whose value depends on another asset.
items.example: Options, futures, and swaps.

items.def: Reducing exposure to a particular risk.
Attempting to profit from price differences between related assets.
Investing based on characteristics historically associated with returns.
items.example: Value, quality, momentum, and size are common factors.
